newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS - Festivals to keep Malaysia interest rates up.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Festivals to keep Malaysia interest rates up.

text.p: Cash withdrawals of up to $1.0 billion for the Moslem Eid al-Fitr and Chinese Lunar New Year festivals next month are expected to keep Malaysian interest rates firm, dealers said on Thursday.
They said banks had begun hoarding cash to allow depositors to withdraw money for the celebrations, reducing liquidity in the banking system and pushing up interbank interest rates in the last week.
Estimates by dealers for withdrawals during the festivals varied from two billion ringgit ($805 million) to three billion ringgit ($1.2 billion).
"Interest rates will remain at the current levels at least until the festivals are over," said the head of money dealing at one of Malaysia's biggest banks.
Once spending for the festivals is over, the money would return to the banking system as deposits, he said.

However the trend could change if the central bank, Bank Negara Malaysia, released new funds or if there were inflows of money as a result of the ringgit's movement in the foreign exchange market, the dealers said.
On Wednesday, the central bank returned some funds to the system, causing a mild decline in interbank rates on Thursday.
Dealers said the funds returned were part of Bank Negara's direct borrowing from selected banks as part of its open market operations.
No confirmation was available from Bank Negara, which does not comment on its money market operations.
A money market dealer with a foreign bank said the market would remain tight for the next one month until the festival season ended in the middle of February.
Dealers said Bank Negara was rumoured to have injected funds into the market late on Monday after the overnight rate broke its perceived upper limit of 8.5 percent.
Last week, the ringgit's nearly two percent rise against the dollar also affected the money market trend. Interest rates eased slightly, only to be pulled up by festival withdrawals.
Dealers said the movement in the foreign exchange market had shifted some of the funds to foreign banks, as locals sold the ringgit against the U.S. dollar during the rally.

The head of money dealing at another bank said these foreign banks had internal restrictions on lending to some institutions considered high-risk borrowers in Malaysia, like finance companies and merchant banks.
"With most institutions short (of short-term money) and a lot of cash sitting in bank vaults, short-term rates are going up," he said.
On Thursday, one-week money was traded in the interbank market at 7.20/30 percent, one-month money at 7.35/38 percent and three-month at 7.35/40 percent.

Malaysia's growing current account deficit and inflation triggered worries about overheating last year and forced it to maintain a tight monetary policy. The three-month interbank rate has risen by nearly 200 basis points in the past two years.
The three-month rate in Malaysia is around four percentage points higher than in neighbouring Singapore.
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-230 8911)
